title: Gathering the corners
hookLine: many gather the four fringes of the prayer shawl before the Shema

cards: If you've ever been in a synagogue on a weekday morning, you might have seen it without knowing what it was.
Partway through the prayers, people wrapped in big striped shawls reach out, one corner at a time, and gather the long knotted fringes into one hand.
Then they hold the bundle close, often against the heart, and keep holding it. It takes a few seconds, and it's timed to one phrase in the blessing.

teach.b: The shawl is a tallit, a prayer shawl. What makes it a tallit isn't the stripes or the fabric.
It's the fringes, tzitzit, tied on its four corners. The Torah commands them in two places.
In Deuteronomy, in the old Jewish translation: "Thou shalt make thee twisted cords upon the four corners of thy covering, wherewith thou coverest thyself." Now, the gesture.
Near the end of Ahavah Rabbah, the blessing asks God: bring us in peace from the four corners of the earth.

The Hebrew word for corners is kanfot, the same word used for the corners of the garment. It can also mean wings. So at those words, many people gather the four fringes from the four corners into one hand.

Scattered threads, brought together, while the prayer asks for a scattered people to be brought together, echoing the prophet Isaiah's picture of gathering the dispersed from the four corners of the earth.
They hold the fringes through the Shema, and in its third paragraph, where the fringes are commanded, many kiss them each time the word tzitzit is said. Who wears one differs by community.
In Orthodox practice it's men, in many Ashkenazi communities from marriage and in many Sephardi communities from boyhood. In many Conservative and Reform communities, women wear one too.
The tallit is usually worn for morning prayer, by daylight.
Wherever the gesture is done, its shape is simple: four corners, one hand.

how: Those who wear a tallit at morning prayer often gather its four fringes at the words 'bring us in peace from the four corners of the earth' near the end of Ahavah Rabbah, hold them through the Shema, and kiss them at each mention of tzitzit.

practice: If you have a tallit, gather its fringes; if not, open your hand. Name four people scattered from you, in another city or out of touch, and curl one finger into your palm for each.
Then hold the closed hand against your chest, and breathe with them there.
